catalog_quote: Hoewel ik in dit opstel niet al mijn gegevens kan verwerken, wil ik hier toch enkele woorden ter aanvankelijke vergelijking laten volgen. Opgemerkt wordt, dat (behalve in het Galéla'sch en Ternate'sch) bijna alle woorden den klemtoon krijgen op de 3e lettergreep van achteren. Waar dit niet het geval is wordt een ' aangegeven.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Opgemerkt wordt, dat (behalve in het Galéla'sch en Ternate'sch) bijna alle woorden den klemtoon krijgen op de 3e lettergreep van achteren. Waar dit niet het geval is wordt een ' aangegeven.
new_statements.translation: It is noted that (except in Galela and Ternate) almost all words receive the stress on the third syllable from the end. Where this is not the case, an ' [acute accent] is marked.
new_statements.citation: Fortgens, J. 1905. Vier weken onder de Tabaru en Waioli van Noord-West Halemahera. Mededeelingen vanwege het Nederlandsch Zendelinggenootschap 49: 1-53.
new_statements.locator: p. 33 (p. 44 of the archive.org volume scan tijdschriftvoor13zendgoog; page scan pages/), the paragraph introducing the comparative lists Tab./Wai./Ib./Gal./Lod., pp. 33-36
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (493-page Google scan of MNZG 49, no text) and re-rendered pp. 44-47 at 200 dpi; p. 44 carries journal page number 33, so the locator is right. The quoted sentence is on that page exactly as given: "Opgemerkt wordt, dat (behalve in het Galéla'sch en Ternate'sch) bijna alle woorden den klemtoon krijgen op de 3e lettergreep van achteren. Waar dit niet het geval is wordt een ' aangegeven." It also appears in the archive.org scanned file (lines 1673-1676). The sentence is the preamble to the comparative lists headed Tab. / Wai. / Ib. / Gal. / Lod. / Holl. (pp. 33-36), so it is meant to cover the Ib. column. Checked the Ib. column on 200-dpi crops (saved as pages/, check_p35a/b, check_p36…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the antepenultimate syllable; words that deviate are printed with an acute on the stressed vowel. In the Ibu column the acutes fall on the penult or final syllable of lomodídi 'two', tumudíni 'seven', na midídi, na luáne 'three (of people)', kaúna 'dog', tubaíe 'young man', duliwú 'hair', náu 'ear', naúo 'fish', nogóna 'who?'; four-syllable words printed without an accent (lomotoala 'five', tuanele 'eight', mosolese 'girl') are therefore antepenultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: Deviating words are marked with an acute; for Ibu these are the ten forms listed above (mostly numerals and body-part nouns with penultimate or final stress); disyllables such as náu, wola, kela, reader cannot bear antepenultimate stress at all, and Fortgens does not say how they are treated beyond the accent marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in a comparative wordlist; the rule is a blanket remark by a missionary after a four-week visit (1905) covering Tabaru, Waioli, Ibu and Loda jointly, with Galela and Ternate explicitly excluded. Ibu data came from a few elderly speakers at Tobae/Ibu River mouth.
new_statements.identity_note: Fortgens 1905 calls the variety 'het Ibu'sch', spoken around the Ibu River mouth (Gam-itji, Gam-lamo, Tobae); Voorhoeve 1988 (PL A-76, p. 185) classifies Ibu as a fifth dialect of Sahu (sahu1245), ~90% cognate with Waioli (waio1238) and Gamkonora; Glottolog keeps it as a separate language ibuu1240 (ISO ibu). The stress statement is a blanket remark covering Tabaru (taba1263), Waioli, Ibu and Loda (lolo1264) together, with Ibu-specific acute-marked exceptions in the lists.

sources.note: Ibu column of the comparative wordlist (pp. 376-407) is taken from Fortgens 1905 (p. 371); p. 372 says Ibu is near disappearance; pp. 408-409 note that Ibu replaces ng by n and that the NH languages differ in stress placement (Galela never shifts stress under suffixation, Tobelo shifts it onto the suffix, Modole stresses the exponents) -- nothing Ibu-specific on stress.
